title: What is the best AI agent to use as a trading mentor?
author: Trader_WaveS
selftext:
I've been using Gemini Pro (Spark) to build out my trading journal by feeding it screenshots, TradingView links, market thoughts, and trade setups. The goal is to build an edge database to refine my system, but the AI is falling short.

My main issue is that it acts like an echo chamber—it constantly agrees with whatever I say instead of challenging bad habits or keeping me accountable. Worse, its visual analysis is inconsistent: it frequently misses key chart mechanics like wick taps, liquidity sweeps, or precise key levels. I spend more time babysitting and correcting its breakdowns than actually learning from them.

I need an analytical AI workflow that acts more like an objective mentor—challenging my logic, catching technical nuances on the chart, and enforcing trade setup rules rather than just validating my bias.

What models, custom setups, or specialized tools are you guys using that actually handle technical chart analysis and strict trade reviews well?

comments.author: Character_Cod_5767
comments.body: Mr. GPT has been my educator, mentor,  and trading buddy since I started trading. I tried to use a bot to trade for me. I didn't like it. I like trading manually. Its why I do it.

replies.author: Trader_WaveS
replies.body: Thanks for the response. I’m currently comparing ChatGPT and Claude to see which model makes the best personal trading copilot. I’m not looking to build an automated trading bot—I plan to execute all trades myself. Instead, I need an AI to act as a thought partner to polish my existing strategy: catching blind spots, identifying recurring execution mistakes, and flagging high-probability setups or edge improvements that I might overlook while focusing on my primary patterns.

comments.author: leroylabs
comments.body: I’d separate chart reading from mentoring instead of asking Gemini Pro (Spark) to do both in one pass. First have it inventory only observable features from a clean TradingView export, including candle timestamps, wick taps, candidate sweep levels, and closes back through those levels. Then run a second prompt that scores the trade against a fixed checklist without seeing your market thoughts until after its verdict. That blinded order should reduce agreement bias and reveal whether the visual extraction itself is failing. When you say it misses liquidity sweeps, are those rules defined numerically or only through annotated examples?

replies.author: Trader_WaveS
replies.body: Do you think I shoudl stick with Gemini for this, or should I move to Claude or GPT?

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body:
The agreeing is the default and prompting "be critical" barely dents it. What worked better for me was taking the opinion out of its job: paste your written setup rules once, then for each trade ask it only to list which rules were met and which were broken, nothing else. It can't flatter you on a checklist.

And I'd stop feeding it screenshots for the precise stuff. Vision models are genuinely bad at exact wick levels, give it the OHLC numbers around the entry instead and the "missed the sweep" problem mostly goes away.

replies.author: Trader_WaveS
replies.body:
I think the problem is I'm making it complex by asking to be too human lol

I will try to start the agent from scratch, changing some skills that I created then. 

Do you think I shoudl stick with Gemini for this, or should I move to Claude or GPT? 

Thank you for the advice btw!

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: I'd move to Claude for this, it's what I use and it holds a checklist without drifting back into cheerleading. the prompt change matters more than the model though, so give the checklist a week on Gemini first. and if you ever want the rules run on paper rather than reviewed, I made Quantradin for that (quantradin.com).

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body: I wouldn't pick a model on reputation, because the setup matters more than the name. Take 20 or so past trades where you already know which rules were broken, run the same checklist and OHLC data through Gemini, Claude and GPT, and see which one matches your own labels most often. Keeping the inputs structured also helps, and that includes event timing (CPI, FOMC, earnings) for the day, where Cymetica's EventTrader is one source. Whichever model wins on that test is the one to stay with.

comments.author: Square-Middle-4474
comments.body:
I appreciate what you are saying. I expressed similar concerns in previous posts and as recently as today. Exactly as you have said point by point. It's lived experience. What is remarkable is the way people defend it as if Jesus just stepped off the bus. I remind my students that "in order to obtain value you have to understand context". This is where traders fail. Here is what I know to be true

1)  You have to learn how to prompt AI, and by "Prompt" I mean that you have to know or learn how to frame your request such that it serves your larger purpose. I was taught this important lesson in a seminar at JPMC where the speaker asked attendees to provide a problem to be solved, then showed how to create the type of prompt that would obtain not just one, but several possible solutions. From that preliminary output, you narrow it down.

2) You have to instruct AI to check its own work product for errors of fact. This has to be done repeatedly. 

3) You have to instruct AI to find errors in its logic (as well as the assumptions you make when you prompt it). AI will not do this on its own.

4) You have to instruct AI to determine what (exactly) constitutes industry accepted Best Practice. Again the language you use is critical. AND no it will not do this on its own.

I teach my students to do this from the beginning. Once they see the difference between what they have been doing and what they get when they take the time to learn how to "Prompt" everything changes. 

Good Luck

I use all the frontier models, but would use Claude Code for anything like this. I use a skill to walk through a structured process for prompt development first, and next other skills after to clarify, flesh out, and create a structured development plan.
